item.title: China's retirees embrace seasonal home rather than check-in tourism
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
GUIYANG, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Every year by late June, 66-year-old Li Donglai resettles into his summer routine in Anshun, a city in southwest China's Guizhou Province. This is not a tourist holiday, but a seasonal life away from his own home. Li, from Chongqing, spends more than two months in Anshun each year, drawn by its mild summer weather, nearby hospitals, and everyday conveniences. He buys vegetables at the local market, takes walks around the neighborhood, and heads out to explore attractions within reach. "I used to think retirement meant staying at home, looking after my grandchildren and remaining in my hometown," he said. "After experiencing seasonal living elsewhere, I realize I can actively choose how to spend my later years." Li is one of a growing number of Chinese retirees who have moved beyond check-in tourism -- a rushed way of sightseeing. They choose the same place to stay for weeks or months each year and build everyday routines there. What begins as a trip becomes a way of living for part of the year. MOVING WITH SEASONS For many retirees, it is the thermometer, not the hometown, that decides where the year is spent. Zhao Tianlong, who runs a seasonal-living center in Yunnan, sees the effect in his clients every year. From June to September, retirees from hot regions such as Hunan, Sichuan and Chongqing head to cooler Yunnan cities like Kunming and Dali. From November to March, retirees from northern China head south to escape the cold. Places in Guizhou, Yunnan, Guangxi and Hainan have become popular destinations, combining comfortable climates with well-developed healthcare, transportation and everyday amenities. In Yunnan alone, local reports show seasonal-living visitors topped 5.51 million in 2025, up 41.4 percent from a year earlier, and stayed an average of 83 days. Li Ying'an, 74, is one of many Chongqing residents who flee the summer heat. He describes life back home as "living in a steamer." He and his wife compared several cities' climates, healthcare and living costs before settling on Qujing in Yunnan, where they have now spent 11 summers. Liu Yufen, from northeast China's Jilin Province, spends her winters in China's southern island province of Hainan to escape the cold and ease her joint pain. "Take a walk in the park next door in the evening, and you'll hear Northeastern accents everywhere," she said. FINDING NEW CONNECTIONS Beyond accommodation, food and sightseeing, seasonal living is also meeting a deeper need for companionship and social connection. Wang Fei, who heads a department serving seasonal residents in Anshun Economic and Technological Development Zone, puts it simply: climate brings retirees to a destination, but social connections can keep them there. For many seniors, retirement can mean a shrinking social circle. Zhao Tianlong said many older people living in high-rise apartments in cities barely know their neighbors, while their children are busy with work and their own families. As a result, they often spend much of the day alone or with their spouse. To bring people together, Zhao has organized paper-cutting, calligraphy, poetry recitation and table tennis at his center. Similar activities have become common in seasonal-living communities, giving retirees opportunities to pursue their interests while making new friends. "Compared with staying in a nursing home, seasonal living gives us more freedom and flexibility. We can decide how to spend our time, socialize and have fun," said Li Ying'an, who formed an arts group in Qujing with fellow retirees from Sichuan and Chongqing. The group rehearses in parks and performs at local events throughout the summer. DEVELOPING NEW MARKET What began as a seasonal escape is now developing into a broader market. According to a report released by the China National Committee on Aging, China recorded 84.316 million senior-living stays from July 2024 to June 2025, averaging 7.026 million a month. The figure counted monthly stays of people aged 60 and above who spent more than 14 days in a city outside their home province, for up to six months a year. Ge Lei, secretary-general of the China Tourism Association, attributes the trend to China's aging population, rising demand for higher-quality experiences and a more supportive policy environment. At the end of 2025, China had 323.38 million people aged 60 or above, accounting for 23 percent of the population. The figure is projected to surpass 400 million around 2035. "This group of people has the time and financial means to enjoy retirement, a strong sense of how they want to live, and a growing demand for wellness and leisure stays away from home," Ge said. Policy support has also helped the sector take shape. In 2021, China included senior tourism and seasonal retirement living in its national development plan. Yunnan, Guizhou, Hainan and other provinces have also introduced local action plans to promote and regulate the sector. As the market grows, destinations are increasingly vying for a share. Jilin, for example, will allocate 100 million yuan (14.83 million U.S. dollars) a year for three consecutive years from 2027 to develop itself as a summer destination for retirees. Kaifeng in Henan Province aims to build partnerships with more than 100 cities by 2027 to share resources and visitors. After seeing the trend unfold in Anshun, Wang believes seasonal living among retirees is moving from a niche choice to a mainstream way of life, and one that is becoming a normal part of retirement in the years ahead. ■

item.title: Europe braces for costly winter as gas buffer thins, energy shock persists
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
* European benchmark gas prices have retreated from their mid-September peak but remain far above last year's levels. * Data from Gas Infrastructure Europe showed EU storage facilities are around 70 percent full. A colder winter depleted inventories, while summer heatwaves increased gas use for power generation. * Noting that Europe was facing a supply-driven price crisis, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen on Friday urged countries to consider measures that sustain storage injections or reduce gas and electricity use where necessary. WARSAW, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Europe is entering its first full heating season since the outbreak of the Iran war, whose impact is rippling beyond natural gas to diesel prices and household and industrial energy costs. Four years of efforts to diversify its energy system have given the European Union (EU) more supply options, but the bloc now faces unusually low gas stocks and greater exposure to global price shocks. The coming heating season will test whether its energy resilience can protect households and industry without another major inflationary hit. ENERGY SHOCK SPREADS European benchmark gas prices have retreated from their mid-September peak but remain far above last year's levels. Dutch TTF front-month gas traded at around 72 to 73 euros (about 81.8 to 83 U.S. dollars) per megawatt hour on Monday, after climbing above 80 euros (90.9 dollars) earlier this month. By comparison, the TTF averaged roughly 32 euros (36.4 dollars) per megawatt hour in September 2025. The energy shock has pushed up inflation. Euro area annual inflation rose to 3.2 percent in August from 2.9 percent in July, according to Eurostat data. Energy prices contributed 1.29 percentage points to headline inflation. The transmission to consumers could also be faster than during the 2022 energy crisis. A European Central Bank survey found that in more than half of the euro area, changes in wholesale gas prices are now expected to pass through to consumer gas inflation within one to three months, faster than four years ago. Businesses are also absorbing higher costs. A survey released in July by the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry found that of around 3,100 companies surveyed, 49 percent reported rising electricity costs, while 67 percent said heating had become more expensive. The strain is no longer confined to gas. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its September oil market report that tightness is now particularly acute in refined products, with diesel prices rising more sharply than crude oil. Net diesel and gasoil exports from Gulf countries averaged about 390,000 barrels per day in August, merely a quarter of pre-war levels, according to the IEA. LOW STOCKS, HIGH RISKS Europe is approaching winter with a much thinner gas buffer than usual. Data from Gas Infrastructure Europe showed EU storage facilities are around 70 percent full. A colder winter depleted inventories, while summer heatwaves increased gas use for power generation. High wholesale prices and an unfavourable seasonal price spread earlier in the year also weakened the commercial incentive to buy gas and store it for winter. Europe nevertheless has more supply routes than it did during the 2022 crisis. In 2025, Norway supplied about 52 percent of the EU's imports of natural gas in gaseous form, followed by Algeria at 17.4 percent, according to Eurostat data. Meanwhile, its gas system has been reshaped by a sharp increase in liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports. LNG now accounts for nearly half of EU gas supply, according to the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators. The United States supplied 58 percent of the bloc's LNG imports in 2025, equivalent to around one quarter of its total gas demand. Such diversification has reduced Europe's dependence on individual pipelines, but also tied it more closely to the global LNG market where cargo availability and prices can change quickly when production or shipping routes are disrupted. The Strait of Hormuz crisis has exposed that vulnerability, with LNG loadings from Qatar and the UAE falling 35 billion cubic meters from a year earlier between March and June, according to the IEA. And Gulf supplies are recovering more slowly than previously forecast. Qatar said repairs to two LNG trains damaged at Ras Laffan would take about three years, although normal operations could resume within weeks once the strait reopens. MOVES TO CUSHION PRICE SHOCK Earlier this month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that disruption around the Strait of Hormuz had cost the EU an additional 90 billion euros (102 billion dollars) in fossil fuel imports, "without a single molecule of energy added." Noting that Europe was facing a supply-driven price crisis, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen on Friday urged countries to consider measures that sustain storage injections or reduce gas and electricity use where necessary. In line with Jorgensen's call, the Dutch government said Friday it plans to maintain a publicly backed strategic gas reserve of 5 terawatt-hours (TWh) a year, enough to cover roughly two weeks of national demand, while requiring suppliers to hold part of their winter needs in physical storage. Other European governments have also taken steps to cushion consumers and shore up energy security. Germany approved a law on Friday to cut energy taxes on petrol and diesel. Taking effect on Oct. 1 and running through the end of the year, the measure is set to cut pump prices by about 17 euro cents (0.19 dollars) per liter, providing some 2.5 billion euros (2.84 billion dollars) in relief. France announced a 450-million-euro (511.21-million-dollar) package to extend assistance to frequent drivers and fuel-intensive sectors, while President Emmanuel Macron called for a G7 energy meeting to coordinate energy stocks, exports and production capacity, as well as to examine the possible release of strategic reserves. (Video reporters: Yang Yuchen, Du Zhiqian, Zhang Zhaoqing, Jin Danyi, Cui Kexin, Liu Baiyun, Shao Haijun, Gao Jingyan, Kang Yi, Chen Yufen, Xie Yuan, Song Jia and Sun Yi; Video editors: Zhang Yucheng, Roger Lott, Zhang Yuhong, Cao Ying, Luo Hui, Liu Ruoshi and Zhang Yueyuan) ■

item.title: Major water conservancy project begins power generation in China's Xinjiang
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
URUMQI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The first batch of generating units of the Dashixia Water Conservancy Project in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region was connected to the grid for power generation on Tuesday, its constructor said. Located in Wensu Grand Canyon in Xinjiang's Aksu Prefecture, the 247-meter-high dam of this water conservancy hub is currently the world's highest concrete-faced sand-gravel dam, according to the constructor, China Gezhouba Group Co., Ltd. When fully operational, the hub can generate over 1.89 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, capable of meeting the electricity needs of approximately 600,000 households. It will also channel 3.42 billion cubic meters of water to the Tarim River each year, easing water shortages on more than 6.8 million mu (about 453,333 hectares) of farmland, while significantly boosting flood control capacity and greatly advancing agricultural modernization in southern Xinjiang. During the construction process, blockchain technologies were applied to collect concrete data and manage transportation, making project quality controllable and traceable, noted Song Xiaojian, the project manager. To mitigate the impact of the project on fish, the constructor also invested 65 million yuan (around 9.64 million U.S. dollars) in various ecological protection measures, which went into operation ahead of schedule, according to Yang Yanling, who is with the project's quality and environmental protection department. So far, a total of 141,000 fish have been released through artificial propagation, Yang added. ■

item.title: China urges the Philippines to stop playing up South China Sea issue in multilateral fora
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy said Monday that the Philippines should stop playing up the South China Sea issue in multilateral fora and should, instead, return to the bilateral track. In exercising the right of reply at the General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, said that with regard to the Philippine statement delivered at the debate on Saturday, China has consistently maintained that the United Nations is not the appropriate forum to discuss the South China Sea issue. However, he said, China finds it necessary to issue a solemn response to the relevant erroneous claims by the Philippines. China's position on the so-called "South China Sea arbitration" has been consistent and clear, Sun said. The Philippines' unilateral initiation of arbitration violates fundamental principles of international law, including state consent and pacta sunt servanda, and contravenes the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, he added. The "arbitral tribunal" exceeded its authority and abused its jurisdiction. The so-called "award" it rendered is illegal, null and void. China neither accepts nor recognizes the "award," and opposes and will never accept any claim or action arising from it, said Sun. This is both to safeguard China's own territorial and maritime rights and interests and to uphold the international maritime rule of law and a fair and equitable international maritime order, he said. The Philippine attempt to play up the 10th anniversary of the so-called "award" is utterly meaningless. The fact is that the "award" has not only failed to resolve the maritime issues between China and the Philippines, but has also exacerbated regional tensions, becoming a stumbling block to China-Philippines relations and to peace and stability in the South China Sea, he said. China does not accept any imposed solution with respect to territorial issues and maritime delimitation disputes, and remains committed to resolving the disputes through negotiation and consultation with countries directly concerned. China will continue to work with members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to jointly safeguard peace and stability in the South China Sea, he said. China urges the Philippines to stop playing up the issue in multilateral fora, return as soon as possible to the right track of bilateral consultations, work with China to manage South China Sea disputes, and work together to safeguard peace and stability in the South China Sea, said Sun. ■

item.title: China Coast Guard patrols waters east of Taiwan Island
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The China Coast Guard (CCG) on Tuesday conducted routine law-enforcement patrols in the waters east of China's Taiwan Island in accordance with the law, a spokesperson said. Jiang Lue, a spokesperson for the CCG, said that a CCG task group led by the ship Zhujiajian has been strengthening control over the relevant waters since September. This is to effectively ensure orderly navigation and activities, and to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests, as well as the lives and property of Chinese people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. The CCG will continue to strengthen law-enforcement patrols in the waters under China's jurisdiction and resolutely safeguard China's territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, the spokesperson said. CCG task groups have maintained routine patrols in the relevant waters over recent months. Also on Tuesday, a spokesperson of the CCG Donghai Branch said the coast guard of east China's Fujian Province has conducted routine law-enforcement patrols in accordance with the law in the waters near Kinmen since the beginning of September. Task groups have been dispatched to strengthen control and management over relevant waters, said Zhu Anqing, adding that the move is an effective step to protect the legitimate rights and interests, as well as the lives and property of fishermen on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, and to ensure orderly navigation and activities. Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu are all parts of China. Law enforcement patrols carried out by the mainland coast guard in the relevant waters are reasonable and lawful, and are conducive to maintaining maritime operational order and protecting people from both sides of the Taiwan Strait. ■

item.title: China expects bumper 2026 grain harvest as agricultural, rural modernization gathers pace
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on accelerating agricultural and rural modernization to drive all-round rural revitalization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai) BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China is on track for a bumper grain harvest in 2026 amid steady progress in agricultural and rural modernization, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs said Tuesday. This year, summer grain output exceeded 150 million tonnes for the first time, and early rice output remained above 28 million tonnes for the sixth consecutive year, the ministry said at a press conference. Autumn crops, the mainstay of China's annual grain production, are now being harvested, with the planted area expanded and that of high-yielding crops, particularly corn, increasing notably, according to Zhang Zhu, minister of agriculture and rural affairs. "Against the backdrop of increased volatility in global grain markets, China has a solid foundation and ample confidence to ensure stable grain production and supply," said Zhang. SOLID FOUNDATION FOR FOOD SECURITY Food security has long been an important priority for China, which feeds nearly one-fifth of the world's population with less than 9 percent of the world's arable land. Ensuring a stable food supply is becoming more challenging amid geopolitical uncertainties and increasingly frequent extreme weather events. Despite the headwinds, China's annual grain output has remained above 700 million tonnes for two consecutive years of 2024 and 2025. Per capita grain availability has surpassed 500 kg, which is higher than the global average. The country has achieved basic self-sufficiency in grains and ensured a secure supply of staple foods, Zhang said. "We are firmly holding the rice bowl of the Chinese people in our own hands." Beyond grains, China is also expanding food sources to ensure a diverse and abundant supply of agricultural products. Last year, China's meat production exceeded 100 million tonnes for the first time, with per capita meat availability reaching about 1.5 times the global average. Per capita egg availability exceeded the level in developed countries. The country aims to ensure that its population of more than 1.4 billion has enough to eat and access to a healthier, more nutritious diet over the five years between 2026 and 2030, said Chen Bangxun, a spokesperson for the ministry. Efforts will be made to advance modern facility-based agriculture, develop more food resources from fisheries, forests and grasslands, and use synthetic biology to create new sources of food, Chen added. TECHNOLOGY DRIVES AGRICULTURAL MODERNIZATION The role of technology in China's agricultural modernization continues to grow, according to the ministry. The contribution of science and technology to agricultural development has now exceeded 64 percent, with innovations such as smart agricultural machinery and agricultural robots increasingly being applied in farming, according to Maierdan Mugaiti, vice minister of agriculture and rural affairs. Such progress is supported by a series of policy measures. The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) sets out specific measures to advance agricultural science and technology and modernize agricultural equipment. The latest move in this regard is a plan for China's agricultural and rural modernization for the same period, which sets a target of raising the contribution of science and technology to agricultural development to 67 percent by 2030. It also calls for wider application of AI in agriculture and breakthroughs in developing new quality productive forces in the sector. China will foster more agricultural technology companies and support them in taking on more research tasks addressing urgent industry needs, Mugaiti said. The country will also accelerate the application of new technologies and the commercialization of agricultural research results to serve the industry and benefit farmers, he noted. CONSOLIDATING POVERTY ALLEVIATION GAINS Consolidating the gains from poverty alleviation and promoting rural development remain key priorities, with a focus on job creation, local industry development, and increasing farmers' incomes, according to the ministry. By 2021, China had lifted 98.99 million rural residents living below the then poverty line out of poverty and announced the completion of its fight against absolute poverty. It then established a five-year transition period from 2021 to 2025 to consolidate and expand those gains and prevent people from falling back into poverty. Over the past five years, development conditions in areas and among people lifted out of poverty have continued to improve, while their capacity for self-development has grown stronger, Zhang said. With the five-year transition period wrapped up, China has entered a new stage of regular, targeted assistance. China has established a nationwide system covering all provinces and the entire rural population to identify people at risk of falling back into poverty and provide targeted assistance. So far, all 2.56 million people identified as being at risk have received assistance, Zhang said. This year, the central government has allocated 177 billion yuan (about 26.26 billion U.S. dollars) to support rural industries, employment and development-based assistance in less-developed areas. This has provided greater support for rural development and helped boost farmers' incomes. The per capita disposable income of rural residents in counties that have been removed from the poverty list rose from 12,588 yuan in 2020 to 18,627 yuan in 2025, achieving average annual growth of 8.2 percent, a State Council report revealed. China is also developing local specialty industries to boost farmers' incomes, the ministry said. Efforts should be made to strengthen agricultural product processing, foster new industries and business forms and develop new types of rural services, said Mugaiti. "We will continue to create more opportunities for farmers to benefit from rural industries, strengthen links between farmers and businesses, create more jobs in rural areas and ensure continued growth in farmers' incomes," he said. ■

item.title: APEC CEO Summit draws strong global interest with U.S. firms leading registration: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- With 50 days remaining until the opening of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026, the event has attracted global attention and strong interest from both Chinese and international companies, with U.S. firms being the most active, China's trade promotion body said Tuesday. U.S. firms have been particularly active in the signing up process and the United States is currently the APEC economy with the largest number of registered companies, said Wang Wenshuai, spokesperson for the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT), at a regular press briefing. American Fortune Global 500 companies and well-known firms, including Amazon, Walmart, Apple, Google, ExxonMobil and Microsoft, have submitted applications to attend, Wang said. Wang added that the U.S. firms applying to attend come from multiple sectors, including semiconductors, artificial intelligence, biopharmaceuticals, energy, finance, transportation, logistics, chemicals, aerospace, manufacturing, consumer retail and other fields. This fully demonstrates the high importance the U.S. business community attaches to participating in Asia-Pacific business cooperation, and the close cooperative relationship between Chinese and U.S. industrial and supply chains, the spokesperson said. China will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, from Nov. 18 to 19. China has chosen the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together" for this year. During the 2026 APEC "China Year," some 300 events are expected to take place across multiple cities in China. Hosted by the CCPIT under the theme "promoting prosperity together for a win-win future," the APEC CEO Summit will bring together around 1,000 political and business representatives from APEC economies. Attendees will discuss topics including the building of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, interconnectivity, artificial intelligence, digital economy, the development of Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and sustainable development, according to Wang. ■

item.title: Xi urges Sichuan University to leverage strengths in serving national strategies
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has urged Sichuan University to leverage its interdisciplinary strengths and play a pioneering and exemplary role in serving national strategies, as he extended congratulations on the 130th founding anniversary of the university. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a reply letter to the university's teachers and students. In the letter, Xi congratulated the university's faculty members, students and alumni on the anniversary. He noted that serving the country with dedication, taking root in western China, and fostering talent through education are fine traditions of Sichuan University. Xi expressed the hope that the university will carry forward its revolutionary legacy, leverage its strengths of interdisciplinary integration across humanities, sciences, engineering and medicine, and contribute to building China into a leading country in education, science and technology, and talent development. The history of Sichuan University dates back to the Sichuan Chinese and Western School founded in 1896, the earliest institution of higher learning in southwest China. ■
